opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a mix of things coming together at the same time. On one side, we were watching what happened with language models, where once the right architectures and enough data existed, progress suddenly accelerated. Robotics felt like it was sitting right before a similar moment. The models were getting good enough. Vision-language models could understand scenes and instructions in a way that just wasn't possible a few years earlier, and you could start connecting that understanding to actions.

On the other side, the hardware was getting dramatically cheaper. A decent robot arm used to cost tens of thousands of dollars, so robotics research was limited to a handful of well-funded labs. Now you can build or buy something capable for a few hundred dollars. When the cost of entry drops like that, the number of people who can experiment explodes, and that's usually when a field takes off.

What was missing, and this is where we felt Hugging Face could really help, was the open ecosystem. In robotics, everyone was rebuilding the same things from scratch: their own data formats, their own training code, their own datasets that nobody else could use. It reminded us a lot of NLP before Transformers became a shared library. So the bet was: if we provide open tools, shared datasets, and affordable open hardware, and make it easy for people to share what they collect and train, the community can do the scaling that no single lab can do alone.

And data is really the core of it. Language models had the internet. Robotics doesn't have an equivalent, so you have to collect it. We thought a large open community, with lots of people recording demonstrations on cheap robots in all kinds of environments, might be one of the best ways to build that internet-scale dataset for the physical world. That combination of better models, cheap hardware, and the possibility of community-driven data is what convinced us the timing was right.

r002.rationale: It describes building an internet-scale dataset for robotics, but does not identify world models trained on internet-scale data as a reason to expect progress.

r003.rationale: It cites open tools and shared training code as part of a missing ecosystem, but does not clearly identify adaptable software as the missing component needed to make robotics work effectively.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was a mix of things coming together at the same time, and some of it was personal.

The first was watching what happened in language. When we started Hugging Face, NLP was this fragmented field where every lab had its own architecture, its own tokenizer, its own benchmark. Then transformers arrived, and suddenly you had one architecture, one pretraining recipe, and the whole community could stack improvements on top of each other. Progress compounded because everyone was building on the same foundation. When I looked at robotics around 2023, it felt like NLP in 2017. Lots of brilliant people, but everyone had a different robot, a different simulator, a different data format, and nothing transferred. And I thought, the same convergence is about to happen here, because the models that are starting to work for robots are basically transformers trained on large multimodal datasets. The recipe is already known. What's missing is the open infrastructure.

The second thing was the data question. For years the argument against learning-based robotics was that you can't collect enough data, because robots are slow and expensive and break. But a few things changed. Teleoperation got cheap. People started sharing datasets instead of hoarding them. And vision-language models gave you a way to bootstrap a lot of understanding of the world from internet-scale data, so the robot-specific data you need is much smaller than people assumed. Once I saw that a single person with a few hundred dollars of hardware could collect a useful dataset in an afternoon, I thought, okay, this is now a community problem rather than a corporate problem. And community problems are what we're good at.

And the third was hardware. The cost of a decent robotic arm or a small humanoid collapsed. Rémi Cadène, who joined us to build LeRobot, kept showing me arms that cost a few hundred euros that you could put on a desk. That's the Raspberry Pi moment. When a grad student or a hobbyist can afford the hardware, you get thousands of people experimenting instead of a few dozen labs, and that's when things start moving fast.

So I wouldn't say I was convinced a breakthrough was guaranteed. It was more that I recognized the pattern: a converging model architecture, a data bottleneck that was loosening, and hardware getting cheap enough to democratize. Every time I've seen those three line up, something big has followed. And I wanted the open-source community to be in the middle of it rather than watching from outside, because if robotics ends up concentrated in two or three companies, I think that's a much worse world than one where everyone can build and inspect and share.

r002.rationale: It cites vision-language models drawing on internet-scale data, but does not identify world models trained on that data as the reason to expect progress.

r003.rationale: It says open infrastructure is missing, but does not identify adaptable software as the missing component.

astra-6.text:
What was exciting to us was the possibility that robotics could follow a similar trajectory to language models. Instead of building a system for one robot and one task, you could start training models that learn across tasks and carry some of that knowledge into new situations.

But that requires more than a good model. You need data, accessible hardware, and a way for people to share what works. That’s where we felt Hugging Face could contribute: making it easier for researchers and developers to build on each other’s work.

So it wasn’t one demonstration that convinced us. It was the sense that those pieces were coming together, and that opening them up could help the whole field move faster.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was the feeling that robotics was starting to look like language models a few years earlier. You could see an opportunity to move from systems built for one very specific task to models that could learn across tasks and robots. And that changes what the field needs: shared datasets, shared tools, and a community that can build on each other’s work.

The exciting question was whether we could help create that open ecosystem. Make it easier to get a robot, collect data, train a model, and share what you learned. I wouldn’t say the breakthrough was guaranteed. But it felt like a moment when making those things accessible could really accelerate progress.
